sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Module purpose and imports
sections.what: Explains the coordinate conventions at the top of the file and loads the part data types.
sections.why: The conventions are needed to read the rotation and position maths correctly.
sections.watch_out: The coordinate note is the only written record of the axis mapping, so keep it current with the code.

sections.name: Document
sections.title: Writer interface
sections.what: Defines the expected shape of the writer object: something that can add one line of IFC text and return its entity number.
sections.why: Lets the same code write into any writer that follows this shape.
sections.watch_out: The writer must return a new number each time, or references between entries break.

sections.name: number
sections.title: Number formatting
sections.what: Writes numbers with twelve decimal places and turns very small values into zero.
sections.why: Keeps the text consistent and avoids writing negative zero.
sections.watch_out: A NaN or infinite value would be written as text that IFC cannot read.

sections.name: placement_values
sections.title: Converting position and rotation to IFC values
sections.what: Turns a viewer position and set of three rotations into nine IFC numbers: the position, an axis direction and a reference direction.
sections.why: Converts the viewer's coordinate convention to the IFC one, so exported parts face the same way as in the viewer.
sections.watch_out: A sign error here moves or mirrors every part, so this is the first place to check after a geometry complaint.

sections.name: placement
sections.title: Building a placement in the IFC file
sections.what: Writes a point, two directions, a frame and a local placement. A parent placement can be given, and it must already exist in the file.
sections.why: IFC needs this chain of entries to position an object.
sections.watch_out: A parent number that does not exist in the file leaves a broken reference.

sections.name: solid
sections.title: Writing a solid shape for a part
sections.what: Writes a rectangle or circle profile, extrudes it by the part's height from its base, and wraps the result in a body shape and a product shape.
sections.why: Viewer primitives are centred on their middle, but IFC extrusions start at the base, so the start is moved down by half the height.
sections.watch_out: Only box and circle are handled. Any other primitive is treated as a circle, using half the x dimension as its radius.

sections.name: geometry_values
sections.title: Geometry values for comparison
sections.what: Returns the primitive name and the three dimensions as text.
sections.why: Likely reason: used to compare or fingerprint part shapes. The calling code is not visible in this file.
sections.watch_out: Values are rounded the same way as in the file, so very small differences are hidden in the comparison.

summary: Converts explicit model parts into IFC text: a placement (position and orientation), a box or circle solid, and the geometry values, while keeping the viewer's coordinate convention.
purpose: Lets exported IFC files show each part at the same position and orientation as the 3D viewer.
why: The module says the viewer uses X right, Y up and Z toward the viewer, while IFC uses X, minus Z and Y. Rotations follow the Three.js convention. No geometry recipe is inferred here.
how: Converts the viewer position and rotation into IFC values. Writes a point, two directions and a frame, and combines them into a local placement. For a shape, writes a profile, extrudes it upward from its base, and links it to a representation and a product shape.
inputs: A part's position, rotation, dimensions and primitive kind, and a writer object that adds IFC lines and returns their numbers.
outputs: IFC lines written to the document with their entity numbers, and plain text values for geometry.
risks: The rotation calculation is the most error-prone part. A sign error would tilt or mirror every part. Any primitive other than box is written as a circle.
debug: Compare one exported part's position with the viewer. If parts sit at the wrong height, check the base offset. If rotated parts look mirrored, check the axis conversion.
